title: Runtime operator cheatsheet: TRT / Triton / custom adapter tradeoffs
content:
Purpose
This is a short, practical operator-facing cheatsheet and running notes for on-call engineers and runtime devs. Focus: when to use TensorRT engine paths, when to go through Triton (server-managed), and when to fall back to our custom-kernel pipeline. Document collects tradeoffs, gotchas, quick checks, and lightweight experiments that surfaced surprising KV-cache and scheduling interactions.

TL;DR (operator summary)
- TensorRT engine path: best for high-throughput stable models with consistent sequence lengths and quantized/FP16 builds. Expect fastest token throughput and smallest per-token GPU compute, but non-trivial cold-start + engine build/deserialize overhead and limited flexibility for dynamic shapes unless we prepare multiple engines.
- Triton server path: good for multi-model host consolidation, easier remote autoscaling, and when you want built-in model control (versions, metrics). Slightly higher per-request overhead vs bare TRT but easier operational controls and fast reloads in many cases.
- Custom-kernel path: best when model needs ops not supported by TRT, for experimental attention changes, or when we need fine-grained control over KV layout and memory. Higher dev/maintenance cost and usually slower than TRT but gives predictable behavior for odd sequence profiles.

Background/context
We run three main inference adapter types in production:
1) TRT-direct: our runtime loads a serialized TRT engine and executes decoding kernels directly through our engine-adapter shim.
2) Triton-hosted: Triton manages the model instance(s), provides health/metrics, and we route requests over gRPC/HTTP. Our adapter wraps the client and maps sessions to Triton model instances.
3) Custom-kernel: our own fused kernels (cuda graphs + custom attention) executed by the runtime without TRT/Triton indirection.
These interact with the KV cache subsystem and the micro-scheduler in different ways — this doc records observed interactions and quick mitigation patterns.

Observed tradeoffs and concrete behaviors (from recent experiments)
- Cold-starts and engine loads
  - TRT engine deserialize + CUDA context warmup cost: 60-120ms on an A100 (depends on engine size). If we need to create a new TRT engine for a model variant (different max_seq or repacked layers) expect a 100-300ms stall first request.
  - Triton model loading is more predictable (containerized lifecycle hooks), typically 80-150ms for model warmup using our warmed snapshot flow. But Triton has additional RPC overhead for each request (~2-4ms).
  - Custom-kernel warmup is fast for small kernels (20-50ms) but may require kernel JIT/graph warm-up for larger fused graphs (70-160ms).

- Runtime memory and fragmentation
  - TRT engines allocate large contiguous GPU memory regions. If host nodes are memory-fragmented due to other processes, TRT will fail to load or OOM (observed on nodes with 5–10% fragmentation). Mitigation: prefer nodes with eviction headroom, or proactively pre-allocate and hold a small pool of engines for popular models.
  - Custom kernels can use smaller, fragmented buffers via our slab allocator but then pay higher bookkeeping overhead.

- KV cache behavior and cross-adapter session stickiness
  - KV cache layout is adapter-specific (different packing/alignment). When a session switches adapter (e.g., fallback from TRT to custom), the KV cache cannot be trivially reused; we either translate (expensive) or invalidate. Observed p99 tail increase when sessions flip adapters mid-conversation.
  - Heuristic that worked: make routing sticky per-session: choose adapter at session start based on predicted sequence-length distribution and model variant, avoid switching unless a clear failure occurs.
  - KV shadowing: keep a lightweight mirrored cache of first N tokens in both layouts so short adapter switches can be warmed without full migration. This is a moderate memory tradeoff but reduces tail latency spikes in practice.

- Batching and micro-scheduler impacts
  - TRT benefits more from large batch sizes and long sequences (amortizes kernel-launchs). For small short-query workloads, Triton + custom path with continuous batching often outperforms TRT due to lower per-request overhead.
  - Scheduler should consider adapter-specific throughput curves. Example: TRT throughput grows superlinearly with batch up to GPU saturation; custom-kernel scales more linearly. A naive global batching policy caused TRT engines to starve custom-kernel tasks in earlier experiments.
  - Suggested heuristic: maintain per-adapter token-per-second (TPS) models and run a weighted fair scheduler for batching windows. For latency-SLO routes, cap batch wait to 10ms and prefer custom/Triton pipelines for sub-8-token requests.

- Quantization and numeric degredation
  - TRT FP16/INT8 builds gave 20-35% per-token speedups in experiments but introduced occasional hallucination noise at extreme tokens for some LLM variants. Always run a guardrail eval set for each quantized engine before rolling.
  - Custom kernels allow mixed-precision control per-op; safer but more engineering cost.

- Fallback patterns and failure modes
  - Common failures: TRT engine load OOMs, Triton model unavailable (OOM or controller restart), custom-kernel kernel timeout/launch failure.
  - Operator-friendly fallback order that balances latency and correctness: 1) TRT (if loaded) -> 2) Triton (warm model) -> 3) Custom (last resort). This keeps fastest path prioritized while preserving continuity.
  - Important: fallback must be session-aware to avoid KV cache thrash. When falling back, do not immediately evict the TRT cache; mark session as in-“fallback” and progressively warm the new adapter.

Mini experiments (how we measured)
- Microbench harness used simple single-token loop timed across 10k iterations, warm/warm+cold tests. Metrics: median single-token latency, p95/p99, GPU utilization, and KV cache hit-rate. All runs on A100-40GB with isolated instance.
- Another test used 500 synthetic sessions with Zipf-length distribution to simulate chat workloads and measured adapter-switch tail behaviour.

Quick operator checklist (when seeing rising p99 or errors)
- Check engine load errors in /var/log/runtime/trt-engine.log and Triton logs. Look for CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY or engine deserialization exceptions.
- Inspect node fragmentation: nvidia-smi topo & free/available GPU memory. If fragmentation > 10%, consider migrating low-priority jobs or restarting node to defragment.
- Confirm session routing: is there an adapter-switch event? Query internal key session-adapter map: /api/sessions/{id}. If switching frequently, enable sticky routing or raise route-level stickiness TTL.
- If p99 spikes with small token lengths, throttle batch-window for TRT pipelines (reduce to 5–8ms).
- Run the KV cache analyzer script (internal) to spot high invalidation rates. High invalidation -> consider KV shadowing for short contexts or pre-warm translation for longer ones.

Open questions / experiments to run next
- Automated engine packing: build engine variants for common max_seq lengths and pick automatically based on observed per-session sequence histograms. Need to measure memory cost of retaining multiple engines vs load latency.
- Adaptive sticky routing: dynamic policy that allows switching only if predicted cost-benefit > threshold (consider KV migration cost).
- Lightweight on-GPU translation for KV cache between TRT and custom layouts: is a GPU memcpy+repack cheaper than full decode fallback for 1–4 tokens? Run microbench.
- Test Triton vs TRT RPC overhead on high QPS bursts with 256-token sequences: does Triton add more than 10% latency at scale?

Notes to self
- Keep this doc short; create a follow-up with quantitative tables once we finish the engine-packing experiment next sprint.
- Add quick reference logs/grep commands here later.

Next steps
- Run the KV shadowing memory-vs-tail-latency sweep (JIRA:RINF-723).
- Prototype small GPU translator for first-8 tokens between layouts. Add perf hooks.
- Add a route-level toggle for sticky-routing TTL in the control plane so product can tune per-customer.

References / artifacts
- runtime perf harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtimes/tree/main/tools/perf-harness
- PR with scheduler weighting prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtimes/pull/412
- Slack discussion for adapter failures: slack:#serving-runtime thread-tts-integration

-- end of cheatsheet --
